claim: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a common, chronic, autoimmune disease characterized by destruction of insulin-producing beta-cells in the pancreas.
source: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a common, chronic, autoimmune disease, characterized by destruction of insulin-producing beta-cells in the pancreas that results in lifelong dependence on exogenous insulin and is associated with a high morbidity and mortality (Atkinson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Atkinson et al., 2014

claim: T1D results in lifelong dependence on exogenous insulin.
source: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a common, chronic, autoimmune disease, characterized by destruction of insulin-producing beta-cells in the pancreas that results in lifelong dependence on exogenous insulin and is associated with a high morbidity and mortality (Atkinson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Atkinson et al., 2014

claim: T1D is associated with high morbidity and mortality.
source: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a common, chronic, autoimmune disease, characterized by destruction of insulin-producing beta-cells in the pancreas that results in lifelong dependence on exogenous insulin and is associated with a high morbidity and mortality (Atkinson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Atkinson et al., 2014

claim: Environmental factors such as being overweight, infections, microbiome composition, and dietary deficiencies have been reported as risk factors for T1D.
source: Environmental factors such as being overweight, infections, microbiome composition, and dietary deficiencies have been reported as risk factors for T1D (Rewers and Ludvigsson, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rewers and Ludvigsson, 2016

claim: The immunological pathogenesis of T1D includes innate inflammation and adaptive immunity, such as enhanced T cell responses.
source: In turn, the immunological pathogenesis (Cabrera et al., 2016) of T1D includes innate inflammation and adaptive immunity, such as enhanced T cell responses (Hundhausen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cabrera et al., 2016 and Hundhausen et al., 2016

claim: Approximately 60 genomic loci have been associated with T1D risk.
source: In the last two decades, large genome-wide association studies (GWAS) performed have underscored the contribution of genetic polymorphisms to T1D for the susceptibility, with ~60 genomic loci associated with T1D risk identified (Barrett et al., 2009; Bradfield et al., 2011; Cooper et al., 2008; Grant et al., 2009; Huang et al., 2012; Onengut-Gumuscu et al., 2015; Ram et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple GWAS citations

claim: T1D GWAS loci show significant enrichment in specific immune-related biological pathways, such as cytokine signaling and T cell activation.
source: While these loci show significant enrichment in specific immune-related biological pathways, such as cytokine signaling and T cell activation (Barrett et al., 2009; Cooper et al., 2008), the functional consequences of many of these loci and genetic variants are still unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations to Barrett et al., 2009 and Cooper et al., 2008

claim: Blood samples were collected from 243 T1D patients of Dutch descent in the 300DM cohort.
source: In the 300DM cohort, we collected blood samples from 243 T1D patients (132 males and 111 females of Caucasian origin), following a previously described methodology (Aguirre-Gamboa et al., 2016; Ter Horst et al., 2016; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section

claim: The 300DM cohort consisted of 132 males and 111 females of Caucasian origin.
source: In the 300DM cohort, we collected blood samples from 243 T1D patients (132 males and 111 females of Caucasian origin), following a previously described methodology (Aguirre-Gamboa et al., 2016; Ter Horst et al., 2016; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated demographic data

claim: Participant ages in the 300DM cohort ranged from 20 to 84 years.
source: Participant's ages ranged from 20 to 84 years.
evidence: Directly stated demographic data

claim: 269 immune-cell traits were measured in the 300DM cohort.
source: In total, we ended up with 269 immune-cell traits for the 300DM cohort.
evidence: Directly stated measurement outcome

claim: IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-8, IL-10, IL-1Ra, and MCP-1 are considered monocyte-derived cytokines and were measured 24 hr after stimulation.
source: Following our previously reported definition (Li et al., 2016), we considered IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-8, IL-10, IL-1Ra, and MCP-1 to be monocyte-derived cytokines and measured them 24 hr after stimulation.
evidence: Based on previous definition from Li et al., 2016

claim: INF-γ, IL-17, and IL-22 are considered T cell-derived cytokines and were measured at 7 days after stimulation.
source: Likewise, we considered INF-γ, IL-17, and IL-22 to be T cell-derived cytokines and measured them at 7 days after stimulation.
evidence: Based on previous definition from Li et al., 2016

claim: DNA samples of 224 Dutch T1D patients were genotyped using the Infinium Global Screening Array.
source: DNA samples of 224 Dutch T1D patients were collected and genotyped using the Infinium Global Screening Array.
evidence: Directly stated methodology

claim: After quality control, 215 samples from the 300DM cohort remained for further analysis.
source: This left 215 samples for further analysis, and these samples show good consistency with European samples from 1000 Genomes data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) according to standard protocol (Anderson et al., 2010).
evidence: Directly stated after quality control procedures

claim: After quality control and merging, 4,304,387 SNPs and 666 individuals remained in the merged cohort (N300DM = 215 and N500FG = 451).
source: We excluded SNPs with low imputation quality (R2 < 0.3) and/or a MAF < 0.01 in all imputed samples and/or HWE p-values < 1 × 10–5 in healthy individuals, leaving 4,304,387 SNPs and 666 individuals in the merged cohort (N300DM = 215 and N500FG = 451).
evidence: Directly stated after quality control and merging procedures

claim: Age significantly associated with 129/269 immune-cell traits.
source: Age significantly associated with 129/269 immune-cell traits and 12/55 cytokine traits, gender associated with 59/269 immune-cell traits and 5/55 cytokine traits, and seasonal effects associated with 121/269 immune-cell traits and 38/55 cytokine traits (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and referenced figure

claim: Age significantly associated with 12/55 cytokine traits.
source: Age significantly associated with 129/269 immune-cell traits and 12/55 cytokine traits, gender associated with 59/269 immune-cell traits and 5/55 cytokine traits, and seasonal effects associated with 121/269 immune-cell traits and 38/55 cytokine traits (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and referenced figure

claim: Gender significantly associated with 59/269 immune-cell traits.
source: Age significantly associated with 129/269 immune-cell traits and 12/55 cytokine traits, gender associated with 59/269 immune-cell traits and 5/55 cytokine traits, and seasonal effects associated with 121/269 immune-cell traits and 38/55 cytokine traits (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and referenced figure

claim: Gender significantly associated with 5/55 cytokine traits.
source: Age significantly associated with 129/269 immune-cell traits and 12/55 cytokine traits, gender associated with 59/269 immune-cell traits and 5/55 cytokine traits, and seasonal effects associated with 121/269 immune-cell traits and 38/55 cytokine traits (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and referenced figure

claim: Seasonal effects significantly associated with 121/269 immune-cell traits.
source: Age significantly associated with 129/269 immune-cell traits and 12/55 cytokine traits, gender associated with 59/269 immune-cell traits and 5/55 cytokine traits, and seasonal effects associated with 121/269 immune-cell traits and 38/55 cytokine traits (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and referenced figure

claim: Seasonal effects significantly associated with 38/55 cytokine traits.
source: Age significantly associated with 129/269 immune-cell traits and 12/55 cytokine traits, gender associated with 59/269 immune-cell traits and 5/55 cytokine traits, and seasonal effects associated with 121/269 immune-cell traits and 38/55 cytokine traits (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and referenced figure

claim: B cell subpopulations cluster separately from T cell, monocyte, and NK cell population clusters.
source: We observed a separation of the B cell subpopulations cluster from the T cell, monocyte, and NK cell population clusters.
evidence: Observed in nonmetric MDS analysis shown in Figure 1B

claim: T cells, monocytes, and NK cells have more interplay than B cells at baseline.
source: This suggests that T cells, monocytes, and NK cells have more interplay than B cells at baseline, which is consistent with our previous finding in a healthy cohort (500FG; Aguirre-Gamboa et al., 2016).
evidence: Inferred from clustering analysis and supported by citation

claim: Cytokine features cluster based on their cellular origins.
source: Furthermore, cytokine features are clustered based on their cellular origins, with a partially overlapping cluster between monocyte-derived cytokines and T cell-derived cytokines (Figure 1C).
evidence: Observed in nonmetric MDS analysis shown in Figure 1C

claim: There is a partially overlapping cluster between monocyte-derived cytokines and T cell-derived cytokines.
source: Furthermore, cytokine features are clustered based on their cellular origins, with a partially overlapping cluster between monocyte-derived cytokines and T cell-derived cytokines (Figure 1C).
evidence: Observed in nonmetric MDS analysis shown in Figure 1C

claim: Positive correlations are observed between monocyte lineages and monocyte-derived cytokines.
source: In line with the functional relationship between immune cells and cytokines, we observed positive correlations between monocyte lineages and monocyte-derived cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-10, IL-1RA, IL-8, and MCP-1) and between T cell subsets and T cell-derived cytokines (IFNγ, IL-17, and IL-22) (indicated by red color in Figure 1D).
evidence: Observed in correlation analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: Positive correlations are observed between T cell subsets and T cell-derived cytokines.
source: In line with the functional relationship between immune cells and cytokines, we observed positive correlations between monocyte lineages and monocyte-derived cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-10, IL-1RA, IL-8, and MCP-1) and between T cell subsets and T cell-derived cytokines (IFNγ, IL-17, and IL-22) (indicated by red color in Figure 1D).
evidence: Observed in correlation analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: Negative correlations are observed between monocyte-derived cytokines production and lymphocyte counts.
source: We also found a negative correlation between monocyte-derived cytokines production in response to four distinct types of stimulations (bacteria, fungi, non-microbial, and TLR ligands) and lymphocyte counts (blue, Figure 1D).
evidence: Observed in correlation analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: Similar correlation patterns between immune cells and cytokines are observed in both T1D patients and healthy individuals.
source: We observed similar correlation patterns in 500FG (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Comparison between 300DM and 500FG cohorts shown in figures

claim: A high abundance of adaptive immune cells at baseline is associated with lower production of monocytes-derived cytokines after stimulation.
source: This correlation is in line with a previous finding that a high abundance of adaptive immune cells at baseline is associated with lower production of monocytes-derived cytokines after stimulation (Kim et al., 2007), and this is not altered by T1D status.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2007

claim: The correlation between adaptive immune cell abundance and monocyte-derived cytokine production is not altered by T1D status.
source: This correlation is in line with a previous finding that a high abundance of adaptive immune cells at baseline is associated with lower production of monocytes-derived cytokines after stimulation (Kim et al., 2007), and this is not altered by T1D status.
evidence: Inferred from comparison between T1D and healthy cohorts

claim: The interrelationships between immune cells and cytokines in response to stimulations are roughly similar between T1D and healthy individuals.
source: Overall, the interrelationships between immune cells and cytokines in response to stimulations are roughly similar between T1D and healthy individuals.
evidence: Summary conclusion from correlation analyses

claim: 63 independent T1D loci from published GWAS were present in the study data.
source: Among these, genetic variants in 63 independent T1D loci were present in our data, and we found that 13 of these 63 were indeed associated with susceptibility to T1D with nominal significance (p-value < 0.05) (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: Directly stated from analysis of GWAS data

claim: 13 of the 63 T1D GWAS loci were associated with susceptibility to T1D with nominal significance (p-value < 0.05).
source: Among these, genetic variants in 63 independent T1D loci were present in our data, and we found that 13 of these 63 were indeed associated with susceptibility to T1D with nominal significance (p-value < 0.05) (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: Directly stated from statistical analysis

claim: T1D GWAS SNPs are enriched in association with T cell traits in the T1D cohort (p-value = 0.007).
source: The p-value shows that the T1D GWAS SNPs are enriched in association with T cell traits in the T1D cohort (p-value = 0.007).
evidence: Supported by permutation analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: 261 out of 269 immune-cell phenotypes are suggestively associated with at least one T1D GWAS locus (p-value < 0.05).
source: A pair-wise association analysis between T1D GWAS loci and immune phenotypes shows that 261 out of 269 immune-cell phenotypes and 53 out of 55 cytokine-stimulation pairs are suggestively associated with at least one T1D GWAS locus (p-value < 0.05, Supplementary file 1d and e).
evidence: Directly stated from association analysis

claim: 53 out of 55 cytokine-stimulation pairs are suggestively associated with at least one T1D GWAS locus (p-value < 0.05).
source: A pair-wise association analysis between T1D GWAS loci and immune phenotypes shows that 261 out of 269 immune-cell phenotypes and 53 out of 55 cytokine-stimulation pairs are suggestively associated with at least one T1D GWAS locus (p-value < 0.05, Supplementary file 1d and e).
evidence: Directly stated from association analysis

claim: The 63 T1D GWAS loci explain significantly more variance in 27 cell sub-proportions compared to random sets of independent SNPs (p-value < 0.05).
source: Compared to random sets of independent SNPs, the 63 T1D GWAS loci explain significantly more of the variance in 27 cell sub-proportions and 15 cytokine production traits (p-value < 0.05, Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B,).
evidence: Supported by permutation-based analysis shown in figures

claim: The 63 T1D GWAS loci explain significantly more variance in 15 cytokine production traits compared to random sets of independent SNPs (p-value < 0.05).
source: Compared to random sets of independent SNPs, the 63 T1D GWAS loci explain significantly more of the variance in 27 cell sub-proportions and 15 cytokine production traits (p-value < 0.05, Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B,).
evidence: Supported by permutation-based analysis shown in figures

claim: The T1D risk allele rs11574435-T is associated with a higher percentage of many CCR5+ CD4+ T cell traits and a lower percentage of CCR5− CD4+ T cell traits.
source: As shown in the heatmap (Figure 2C, arrowhead), one T1D risk allele, rs11574435-T, which is in strong LD (r2=0.95) with the T1D GWAS SNP rs113010081 (Onengut-Gumuscu et al., 2015), is associated with a higher percentage of many CCR5+ CD4+ T cell traits and a lower percentage of CCR5− CD4+ T cell traits.
evidence: Observed in QTL analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: rs11574435-T is in strong LD (r2=0.95) with the T1D GWAS SNP rs113010081.
source: As shown in the heatmap (Figure 2C, arrowhead), one T1D risk allele, rs11574435-T, which is in strong LD (r2=0.95) with the T1D GWAS SNP rs113010081 (Onengut-Gumuscu et al., 2015), is associated with a higher percentage of many CCR5+ CD4+ T cell traits and a lower percentage of CCR5− CD4+ T cell traits.
evidence: Directly stated LD relationship with citation

claim: CCR5, CCL5, and CCL4 show significant expression changes in T1D patients compared to controls.
source: This identified significant expression changes of CCR5, CCL5, and CCL4 in T1D patients, which suggests the involvement of this chemokine ligand-chemokine receptor pathway (Figure 3A).
evidence: Observed in transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: The minor allele T in rs35092096 associates with a higher ratio of CCR6+ CCR7− CCR5+ Tregs/CCR6+ Tregs.
source: For example, minor allele T in rs35092096 associates with a higher ratio of CCR6+ CCR7− CCR5+ Tregs/CCR6+ Tregs (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Observed in QTL analysis shown in Figure 3B and C

claim: CCR6+ CCR7− CCR5+ Tregs and T1D share the same regulatory genomic region (H3=0.95).
source: The result strongly supports that CCR6+ CCR7− CCR5+ Tregs share the same regulatory genomic region with T1D, although the causal SNP might be different (Figure 3D, H3=0.95).
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: The CCR region plays a role in Treg function in the pathogenesis of T1D.
source: Altogether, these results support a role for the CCR region in Treg function in the pathogenesis of T1D.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including QTL and colocalization analyses

claim: T1D GWAS loci influence immune-cell proportion and cytokine production capacity.
source: Overall, we observe that T1D GWAS loci influence immune-cell proportion and cytokine production capacity, again stressing the importance of T cell immunity in genetic regulation of T1D.
evidence: Summary conclusion from multiple analyses

claim: Nine genome-wide significant QTLs (p-value < 5 × 10–8) associated with immune-cell proportion were identified in 300DM.
source: To further explore potential genetic regulation of immune phenotypes on the whole-genome level, we performed QTL mapping in 300DM. This identified nine genome-wide significant QTLs (p-value < 5 × 10–8) associated with immune-cell proportion, including four associated with T cell subpopulations expressing specific chemokine receptors (e.g., rs35092096 and rs7614884) (Figure 4A, top and middle panels, Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: Directly stated from QTL mapping analysis

claim: Four of the nine immune-cell proportion QTLs are associated with T cell subpopulations expressing specific chemokine receptors.
source: This identified nine genome-wide significant QTLs (p-value < 5 × 10–8) associated with immune-cell proportion, including four associated with T cell subpopulations expressing specific chemokine receptors (e.g., rs35092096 and rs7614884) (Figure 4A, top and middle panels, Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: Directly stated from QTL mapping analysis

claim: Cell proportion QTLs show significant enrichment in chemokine and cytokine signaling-related biological pathways (FDR < 0.05).
source: Pathway analysis of the cell proportion QTLs showed significant enrichment in chemokine and cytokine signaling-related biological pathways (FDR < 0.05, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), highlighting the effects of immune signaling genes in cell proportion regulation.
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in figure

claim: Six significant genomic loci associated with cytokine production in response to stimulations were detected in 300DM.
source: In parallel, we detected six significant genomic loci associated with cytokine production in response to stimulations by QTL mapping in 300DM (Figure 4A, bottom panel, Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: Directly stated from QTL mapping analysis

claim: Cytokine production QTLs are significantly enriched in TLR-related pathways (FDR < 0.05).
source: Cytokine production QTLs are significantly enriched in TLR-related pathways (FDR < 0.05, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in figure

claim: The missense variant rs5743618 on the TLR1 gene affects IL-6 production in response to S. pneumoniae in PBMC.
source: A missense variant, rs5743618, on the TLR1 gene, affects IL-6 production in response to S. pneumoniae in PBMC.
evidence: Directly stated from QTL analysis

claim: The TLR locus has a strong effect on cytokine levels in controls.
source: Previously, we had observed that the TLR locus has a strong effect on cytokine levels in controls (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2016

claim: TLRs detect pathogens (including bacterial pathogens) and trigger the release of inflammatory cytokines.
source: Our results support the reported function of TLRs in detecting pathogens (including bacterial pathogens) and triggering the release of inflammatory cytokines (Fitzgerald and Kagan, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fitzgerald and Kagan, 2020

claim: A meta-analysis integrating QTLs from 300DM and 500FG cohorts identified 10 novel genetic loci associated with immune-cell proportion.
source: Next, to identify the consistent immune phenotype QTLs within T1D patients and healthy individuals and expand our understanding of genetic regulation of immune phenotypes, we performed a meta-analysis by integrating the QTLs obtained from the 300DM and 500FG cohorts. In total, we identified 10 novel genetic loci associated with immune-cell proportion (Figure 4A, top panel, colored in red) and three novel genetic loci that were associated with cytokine production (Figure 4A, bottom panel, colored in red).
evidence: Directly stated from meta-analysis

claim: A meta-analysis integrating QTLs from 300DM and 500FG cohorts identified three novel genetic loci associated with cytokine production.
source: In total, we identified 10 novel genetic loci associated with immune-cell proportion (Figure 4A, top panel, colored in red) and three novel genetic loci that were associated with cytokine production (Figure 4A, bottom panel, colored in red).
evidence: Directly stated from meta-analysis

claim: The CD5 locus is significantly associated with IgD+ CD5++ proportion in B cells.
source: This included a CD5 locus that was significantly associated with IgD+ CD5++ proportion in B cells (Supplementary file 1F), which may be important as recent studies have reported the relevance of IgD+ CD5++ B cells in T1D (Saxena et al., 2017) and other autoimmune diseases such as Graves' disease (Van der Weerd et al., 2013).
evidence: Directly stated from QTL analysis with supporting citations

claim: IgD+ CD5++ B cells are relevant in T1D.
source: This included a CD5 locus that was significantly associated with IgD+ CD5++ proportion in B cells (Supplementary file 1F), which may be important as recent studies have reported the relevance of IgD+ CD5++ B cells in T1D (Saxena et al., 2017) and other autoimmune diseases such as Graves' disease (Van der Weerd et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Saxena et al., 2017

claim: IgD+ CD5++ B cells are relevant in Graves' disease.
source: This included a CD5 locus that was significantly associated with IgD+ CD5++ proportion in B cells (Supplementary file 1F), which may be important as recent studies have reported the relevance of IgD+ CD5++ B cells in T1D (Saxena et al., 2017) and other autoimmune diseases such as Graves' disease (Van der Weerd et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Van der Weerd et al., 2013

claim: 28 genetic loci were identified as associated with either immune-cell traits or cytokine production phenotypes.
source: To summarize, we identified 28 genetic loci associated with either immune-cell traits or cytokine production phenotypes.
evidence: Summary of QTL mapping results

claim: 11 of the 28 identified loci contain genes that are known drug targets.
source: Among them, the genes within 11 loci (±250 kb window) are known drug targets according to the public drug database (Finan et al., 2017), including COL13A1, CCR family genes, ROR2, NOS1, IL-10, IL-6, STK33, NELL1, FCGR2A, CD5, and TLR1 (Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: Identified through drug database search with citation

claim: STK33 inhibitor is used for rheumatoid arthritis treatment.
source: Some of these genes are already therapeutic targets in other autoimmune diseases, for example, the STK33 inhibitor for rheumatoid arthritis treatment (Rolf et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rolf et al., 2015

claim: 12 out of the 28 significant loci have never been reported in other healthy individual population cohorts.
source: It is also worth mentioning that, as far as we know, 12 out of the 28 significant loci we identified have never been reported in other healthy individual population cohorts according to PhenoScanner V2 (Kamat et al., 2019) (p-value < 1 × 10–5, November 2019).
evidence: Identified through database search with citation

claim: 12 of the 28 significant loci were not identified in the 500FG cohort (p-value < 0.05).
source: Nor were they identified in the 500FG cohort (p-value < 0.05).
evidence: Directly stated from comparison analysis

claim: rs4744112 located on chromosome 9 influences CCR6+ CXCR3+ CCR4− Th1-like helper proportion.
source: One example effect of one of these T1D-specific loci is that of rs4744112 located on chromosome 9, which influences CCR6+ CXCR3+ CCR4− Th1-like helper proportion (Figure 4B), with minor allele G leading to a decrease in these cells relative to major allele T (Figure 4C).
evidence: Observed in QTL analysis shown in Figure 4B and C

claim: The minor allele G of rs4744112 leads to a decrease in CCR6+ CXCR3+ CCR4− Th1-like helper cells relative to major allele T.
source: One example effect of one of these T1D-specific loci is that of rs4744112 located on chromosome 9, which influences CCR6+ CXCR3+ CCR4− Th1-like helper proportion (Figure 4B), with minor allele G leading to a decrease in these cells relative to major allele T (Figure 4C).
evidence: Observed in QTL analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: rs4744112 is located within the transcriptional starting site and enhancer regions of ROR2.
source: rs4744112 is located within the transcriptional starting site and enhancer regions (Kundaje et al., 2015) of ROR2.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kundaje et al., 2015

claim: SNPs within the 28 immune parameter QTLs are mostly located in intergenic and intronic regions.
source: We noticed that SNPs within the 28 immune parameter QTLs are mostly located in intergenic and intronic regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the genetic variants we identified influence immune phenotypes through regulatory effects rather than by altering protein structure alteration.
evidence: Observed in genomic annotation analysis shown in figure

claim: The genetic variants identified influence immune phenotypes through regulatory effects rather than by altering protein structure.
source: We noticed that SNPs within the 28 immune parameter QTLs are mostly located in intergenic and intronic regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the genetic variants we identified influence immune phenotypes through regulatory effects rather than by altering protein structure alteration.
evidence: Inferred from genomic location analysis

claim: 7 out of the 28 loci influence gene expression in blood.
source: Moreover, according to public databases (Carithers and Moore, 2015; Westra et al., 2013), 7 out of the 28 loci influence gene expression in blood (Supplementary file 1F), including rs7512140: FCGR2B/FCRLB, rs35092096: CCR1/CCR3, rs4744112: ROR2/SPTLC1, rs10840031: TRIM66, rs800139: C11orf21, rs1518110: IL10, and rs56350303: AC091814.2.
evidence: Identified through eQTL database search with citations

claim: There is a correlation between baseline immune-cell populations and ex vivo cytokine production in response to bacterial, fungal, non-microbial, and TLR ligand stimulations in T1D patients.
source: The results confirm a correlation between baseline immune-cell populations and ex vivo cytokine production in response to bacterial, fungal, non-microbial, and TLR ligand stimulations.
evidence: Summary conclusion from correlation analyses

claim: There is a direct link between T1D GWAS loci and immune functionality, particularly through circulating T cell subpopulations.
source: We provide evidence for a direct link between T1D GWAS loci and immune functionality, particularly through circulating T cell subpopulations.
evidence: Summary conclusion from multiple analyses

claim: T cell alteration is largely driven by T1D genetics.
source: We show that T cell alteration is largely driven by T1D genetics, while B cells do not show a significant association with T1D GWAS loci.
evidence: Summary conclusion from association analyses

claim: B cells do not show a significant association with T1D GWAS loci.
source: We show that T cell alteration is largely driven by T1D genetics, while B cells do not show a significant association with T1D GWAS loci.
evidence: Summary conclusion from association analyses

claim: The association between the proportion of CCR5+ Tregs and T1D susceptibility through CCR genes suggests that T1D-associated genetic variants contribute to alteration of immune function through a cumulative effect.
source: The association between the proportion of CCR5+ Tregs and T1D susceptibility through CCR genes suggests that T1D-associated genetic variants contribute to alteration of immune function through a cumulative effect.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence

claim: 12 immune phenotype QTLs are specific to 300DM.
source: Finally, out of 28 genome-wide significant genetic loci regulating immune-cell proportions and cytokine production, we identified 12 immune phenotype QTLs specific to 300DM.
evidence: Summary of comparative analysis between cohorts

claim: 11 druggable genes were identified as candidates for therapeutic intervention.
source: We also found 11 druggable genes as candidates for therapeutic intervention.
evidence: Identified through drug database search

claim: Steady-state immune-cell abundance and alteration of immune-cell proportion affect immune response.
source: The correlation we found between baseline immune cells and cytokine production in response to bacterial, fungal, non-microbial, and TLR ligand stimulations suggests that steady-state immune-cell abundance and alteration of immune-cell proportion also affect immune response.
evidence: Inferred from correlation analysis

claim: Immune response variability could be partly explained by variations in steady state.
source: This finding has two important consequences: (1) immune response variability could be partly explained by variations in steady state and (2) treatment of steady-state immune cells before stimulation could also influence immune response after stimulation.
evidence: Inferred from correlation findings

claim: Treatment of steady-state immune cells before stimulation could influence immune response after stimulation.
source: This finding has two important consequences: (1) immune response variability could be partly explained by variations in steady state and (2) treatment of steady-state immune cells before stimulation could also influence immune response after stimulation.
evidence: Inferred from correlation findings

claim: Immune-related genes are physically located in T1D loci or are differentially expressed.
source: Studies comparing T1D patients and healthy controls show that immune-related genes are physically located in T1D loci or are differentially expressed.
evidence: Summary of previous studies

claim: T cell immunity is important in T1D pathology.
source: More studies highlight the importance of T cell immunity in T1D pathology (Farh et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Farh et al., 2015

claim: The occurrence of auto-antibodies in T1D patients has limited pathophysiological relevance and is merely a marker of an autoimmune process mainly driven by T cells.
source: It is thus tempting to speculate that the occurrence of auto-antibodies in T1D patients has limited pathophysiological relevance and is merely a marker of an autoimmune process mainly driven by T cells, as has been suggested before (Martin et al., 2001).
evidence: Speculative interpretation with supporting citation

claim: The effects of different GWAS loci on immune phenotypes vary.
source: Importantly, we reveal that the effects of different GWAS loci on immune phenotypes vary.
evidence: Observed from analysis of effect sizes

claim: The CCR locus has strong effects on immune phenotypes (mean absolute effect sizes = 0.017 for cell proportion and 0.15 for cytokine production).
source: Despite the strong effects of the CCR locus (mean absolute effect sizes = 0.017 [cell proportion] and 0.15 [cytokine production]), we observed much weaker individual effects for other T1D GWAS loci on immune-cell proportion parameters (mean absolute effect size = 0.0060) and/or cytokine production (mean absolute effect size = 0.10) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated from effect size analysis

claim: Other T1D GWAS loci have weaker individual effects on immune-cell proportion parameters (mean absolute effect size = 0.0060).
source: Despite the strong effects of the CCR locus (mean absolute effect sizes = 0.017 [cell proportion] and 0.15 [cytokine production]), we observed much weaker individual effects for other T1D GWAS loci on immune-cell proportion parameters (mean absolute effect size = 0.0060) and/or cytokine production (mean absolute effect size = 0.10) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated from effect size analysis

claim: Other T1D GWAS loci have weaker individual effects on cytokine production (mean absolute effect size = 0.10).
source: Despite the strong effects of the CCR locus (mean absolute effect sizes = 0.017 [cell proportion] and 0.15 [cytokine production]), we observed much weaker individual effects for other T1D GWAS loci on immune-cell proportion parameters (mean absolute effect size = 0.0060) and/or cytokine production (mean absolute effect size = 0.10) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
